claims.text: Conventional casting produces a comparatively coarse-grained high-entropy alloy with limited precipitate distribution.
Additive manufacturing with rapid cooling followed by controlled heat treatment produces a refined grain structure.
Additive manufacturing with rapid cooling followed by controlled heat treatment produces a more uniform dispersion of fine precipitates.
The rapid solidification intrinsic to additive manufacturing suppresses elemental segregation.
A tailored post-processing heat treatment induces nanoscale precipitate formation.
The refined grain structure and uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation movement.
The refined microstructure and precipitate distribution limit grain-boundary sliding or migration.
Obstructing dislocation motion and grain-boundary migration enhances high-temperature strength and creep resistance.
The additively manufactured and heat-treated alloy will have greater elevated-temperature yield strength than a conventionally cast alloy.
The additively manufactured and heat-treated alloy will have greater creep resistance than a conventionally cast alloy.
The expected improvement in yield strength and creep resistance is approximately 15–20% relative to conventionally processed alloys.
The predicted improvement primarily applies between 600°C and 800°C.
The predicted improvement applies under extreme-service conditions relevant to aerospace turbine components, including oxidative atmospheres and high thermal gradients.
The effects outside the 600–800°C service range are uncertain.
